description.ncbi_summary: Aldehyde oxidase produces hydrogen peroxide and, under certain conditions, can catalyze the formation of superoxide. Aldehyde oxidase is a candidate gene for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. [provided by RefSeq, Jul 2008].

uniprot_function.text: Primarily catalyzes oxidation reactions of a broad range of drug and xenobiotic substrates and participates in their metabolism through oxidative biotransformation (PubMed:14709625, PubMed:20444863, PubMed:22279051, PubMed:22996261, PubMed:23857892, PubMed:26322824, PubMed:26842593, PubMed:34415167, PubMed:7786031, PubMed:9224775). Oxidizes at least three structural types of substrates: aldehydes such as benzaldehyde, retinal, pyridoxal, and vanillin; aromatic azaheterocyclic compounds such as phthalazine, quinazoline and phenanthridine; and quaternary azaheterocyclic compounds such as 1-methylnicotinamide and nicotine imine (PubMed:14709625, PubMed:22279051, PubMed:22996261, PubMed:23857892, PubMed:26322824, PubMed:26842593, PubMed:34415167, PubMed:7786031, PubMed:9224775). Converts aldehydes to carboxylic acids, aromatic and quaternary azaheterocyclic compounds to lactams, typically by using molecular oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor and producing hydrogen peroxide as a by-product (PubMed:14709625, PubMed:22279051, PubMed:22996261, PubMed:23857892, PubMed:26322824, PubMed:26842593, PubMed:34415167, PubMed:7786031, PubMed:9224775). Under some conditions, especially with electron-deficient substrates or limited oxygen, can also catalyze reduction reactions using N-methylnicotinamide, 2-hydroxypyrimidine or benzaldehyde as electron donor substrate (Probable) (PubMed:15720138). These reductive activities include N-O bond reductions in nitro groups (e.g., imidacloprid, IMI), hydroxamic acids, and oxazoles (e.g., zonisamide), as well as N-S bond reductions of sulfoxides (e.g., sulindac) (By similarity).
